audio_caption: The clip begins with a cheerful male voice announcing "Hi! I'm Ash, welcome back to my channel." He states that he'll show how to make a specific sound. Immediately following this statement, upbeat electronic music starts, providing a vibrant, energetic backdrop. After the short music sample stops, the male speaker returns, explaining he'll use stock plugins, and then clarifies that he will use Serum because "every producer should have Serum." He praises the plugin's versatility and affordability, and even mentions rent-to-own options, humorously calling out Splice with an optimistic tone.

The audio clip begins with a male speaker stating, "We're going to get into it, let me show you how this is done." A musical vocal chop then starts, followed by the speaker explaining that it's a vocal chop, sourced from an acapella with cool melodies. After this explanation, an acapella is briefly heard with a female vocalist singing, "You never wait for me."

The clip begins with a light, high-pitched female voice singing "all the way for me". A male speaker then takes over, his tone is instructional as he discusses the process of vocal manipulation, specifically transposing audio to a key and using semitones. His explanation shifts to a desire to avoid "chipmunk vocals" and to achieve a "nice, happy medium." The singing then returns, with a high-pitched female voice again singing "all the way for me". The speaker rejects that, "Don't want that at all". A snippet of vocals follows, sung by an unknown voice. The clip concludes with the speaker sharing a technical aspect of their process; "I could wait a thousand days", as he tries to find a "nice tone".

The audio clip begins with a male speaker describing how he tries to find cool vocal chops inside a sample, adding that he'll "go around, pick random spots," followed by some musical snippets that sound like vocal samples. The speaker then describes that he is "looking for stuff that has really nice transients and a lot of syllables." More vocal sample snippets follow, as the speaker describes the value of finding spaces, timings, etc. in such samples.

The audio clip begins with a single male speaker providing instructions about vocal samples, advising listeners to avoid "really long, wobbly notes." An example of such a note is sung, followed by a description of notes with "wonky timing", accompanied by another sung example. The speaker explains assembling the samples into a "normal vocal chop," describing it as "something catchy" before demonstrating an example of this final product, featuring a fast-paced rhythm in a style reminiscent of electronic music.

The audio begins with a male speaker giving instructions on composing music. He states, "you're taking this acapella and making your own melody," and explains that he will make a chord progression along with the acapella. The speaker's tone is instructional and clear. Then the clip transitions into an electronic music style, with synthetic instruments creating a slightly melancholic mood. The speaker states "needs to complement your writing the chord progression for the vocal shop" over the top of the music. The music fades out and cuts out.

The clip begins with mellow jazz music playing in the background, featuring piano chords and an overall relaxed mood. This transitions to speech as a male voice begins discussing musical elements and chords he is using, stating "for reference, the chords I used are..." The tone is informative and technical. The music continues at a lower volume beneath the speech. The same male voice then transitions into a different context, instructing someone to "rename this carrier and then deactivate it. Get rid of it" The speaker sounds assertive.  Another male voice then expresses surprise and questions the instruction, with a tone of disbelief ("What? Why on earth would I do that?"). Finally, the initial male voice calmly responds ("Chill, we're going to get to that"), with a soothing and reassuring tone.

The clip begins with a high-pitched, synthesized "Wub" sound, followed by a male speaker describing how he was trying to recreate it, explaining his attempts to chop and stack vocals, shifting semitones, and using samplers with MIDI. His tone is conversational and narrative as he recounts his failures, humorously stating, "Everything I made sounded like hot garbage." He sets up the next part of his story by describing a show in Montreal.

The clip begins with a male speaker reminiscing about hanging out with producers at a hotel. He recounts a "feast of McDonald's" brought by Uber Eats, and how the topic of "vocal chops" arose. He then recalls a "talented German dude" uttering a single word, "Vocalizer." Immediately following his word, a sound resembling a squealing or high-pitched screech occurs, abruptly cutting off the speech.

The audio clip begins with an enthusiastic "love it", launching into a descriptive summary of audio production. The speaker, a man with a bright and energetic tone, begins breaking down the "good stuff" from the sound setup, specifically focusing on components like "vocoder", "OTT", and "auto pan". The discussion zeroes in on the function of the vocoder and how it processes sound, adding harmonics based on chosen chords. This segment is punctuated by a brief musical interlude, a "rad" electronic piece rich in harmonics, which serves as an example of the explained effects.

The clip begins with a male speaker outlining his intention to use OTT to "thicken it up." This is followed by a quick burst of electronic music with a high-pitched, energetic sound. The speaker then discusses dragging the dry/wet mix to balance vocal chop and harmonics. We then hear more of the same music, with vocal chops dominating the sound. The speaker returns, explaining his choice to use OTT first, to enhance harmonics. The music repeats, alternating between a stripped-down version with fewer harmonics and a richer one. Suddenly, the music stops, replaced by what sounds like a comical telephone call. A panicky, high-pitched female voice calls out, "Hello, excuse me!" A deeper male voice asks what's happening. The female voice accuses someone of copying sounds to prevent other producers from being unique. Finally, a male voice dryly responds, "Said no one ever."

The clip begins with a single male speaker with an informal and informative tone, introducing the purpose of the tutorial to illustrate sound design, emphasizing "finding a unique sound" and how to learn and "put your own twist" on existing techniques. He promises techniques at the end to "make it your own," before returning to the tutorial. This is followed by a brief interlude of electronic music, exhibiting a synthesized, almost otherworldly sound with vocoder elements. The speaker then resumes, continuing his explanations about vocoder settings, mentioning adjusting the levels of bands and cutting out "the mids" for balance. The electronic music returns, now with auto-panning effect that adds movement. The speaker explains it could be the original is "already super cool".

The audio begins with speech, a male speaker explains the basis of a sound and automation, mentioning Ableton. Speaking with an instructional tone, he describes the automation of the rate, keeping it at a default of "1/8", with "little 1/16" touches. He also mentions automating the amount and keeping it at "around 80%", emphasizing balance, finding movement, and turning it off at points for certain notes to "breathe." The speaker highlights that it's a "bit of trial and error," involving listening back to the loop to identify spots for waviness or stops, advising that it becomes a matter of practice. The speech is punctuated by electronic music featuring a prominent synth effect that coincides with the speaker's explanations.

The clip starts with a man stating "That's the sound, that's it," in an informative tone, followed by him talking about EQ and reverb. The music then begins, a bass-heavy trap style, energetic in mood. The speaker describes adding trap drums with a "fake drop" and then refers to an "808". The trap music continues until the man returns, chuckling and saying "There you have it, that's it," followed by a mention of discussing "cool stuff you can do to the sound" and how to "make it your own". He mentions going back into serum.

The audio clip begins with male speech suggesting, "You can actually turn the unison up" and encouraging sound design experimentation. Following this, there is a short burst of a synthesizer-based musical phrase with a glitchy, futuristic, and slightly distorted sound. The male speaker returns, describing the addition of effects to the sound, and cautioning against overdoing sound design. He suggests focusing on minor adjustments and highlights the importance of the vocoder. Next, he discusses the ability to modify sounds within the vocoder. Short musical snippets are played to demonstrate sound effects, including changes to the vocal formant and adjustments to dry/wet settings. Additionally, he describes blending synth sounds and manipulating the vocal to achieve desired effects. The clip concludes with the male speaker encouraging continued experimentation.

The clip begins with a male speaker concluding an explanation, and inviting listeners to "like, subscribe, hit that bell". He encourages engagement, asking to hear what people are making with the sound, and shares his links. He makes a self-deprecating joke about needing validation, and confirms the project file is free. He mentions "stock plugins" and a need for "Serum" before expressing thanks, and signing off with "catch you on the next one, peace". This speech is followed immediately by a section of energetic electronic dance music (EDM). The music features prominent synth melodies, a driving beat, and an overall upbeat and intense mood.
